catalog_locator: printed pp. 8-9 (= PDF pp. 8-9), English Introduction 'Alphabet (a) Vowels' (page images viewed by the third reader); grammar sketch printed pp. 10-11 and p. 17…
catalog_quote: It is essential to stress the right vowel in a word. For instance túwan "his older brother" tuwán "his older brothers" imóm "he drank it" (transitive) ímoum "he is drinking" (intransitive) Stress is indicated in this dictionary, but we do not write it in Muyuw books. ... Unstressed vowels are frequently dropped, especially from long words. ... Unstressed vowels in the early syllables of long words may be dropped completely or partially.

audit.recode_to: PENULTIMATE default (right-edge, weight-insensitive) with morphologically conditioned final stress (transitive verbs with zero 3sg object, where the final stem vowel is elided and stress stays on the old penult; non-inclusive plural of inalienably possessed kin nouns, e.g. túwan/tuwán; monosyllabic transitive stems ibɛ́s vs prefix-stressed intransitives ímad) - i.e. positional-penult + morphological, not lexical. Cite Lithgow & Lithgow 1973 ms pp. 6-8 and Lithgow 1978 pp. 21-24, 31 alongside the 1974 dictionary pp. 8-11, 17; strength of the evidence page-image for all.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on printed p. 8 (image viewed) with the remainder on p. 9 (two scanned layers); locator and citation are correct. (2) The deciding source is a 1974 SIL dictionary front-matter that marks stress per entry but states no rule; lexical was an inference from silence, and the third reader already flagged set by morphology as defensible. (3) The same authors' descriptive papers, downloaded now from the SIL archive via the Internet Archive, do address position: the 1973 'Muyuw verbs' ms has a 'Stress rule' section saying stress is penultimate and 'predictable (penultimate syllable) in an overwhelming majority of words', with surface-final stress in transitive 3sg-object forms explained by final-vowel elision; Lithgow 1978 (published, WPNGL 25) marks stress on the penult in every polysyllabic 'common pattern' noun it lists and shows the prefix-vs-stem alte

sources.quote: p.6: 'Pure intransitive verb stems ... í-gig "he laughs", í-kʌlivʌ́tɔw "he falls". Note that in these verbs the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. As it does in transitive verbs with an objective suffix, e.g. i-gútu-gw "He pulls me out". But if the object is third person singular the suffix is zero. Together with the rule that the final stem vowel is elided this yields the form i-gút-Ø "he pulls it out".' p.7: 'When no object is present, i.e. when the transitive verb is used intransitively, the stress follows the rule: on the penultimate syllable, e.g. í-gut "he pulls out" ... these ver
sources.locator: pp. 6-8, section headed 'Stress rule' and start of 'Morphophonological changes' (page images viewed)
sources.note: Contains an explicit 'Stress rule' section (pp. 6-8): penultimate stress 'predictable.. in an overwhelming majority of words', transitive 3sg forms final-stressed via final-vowel elision - directly contradicts the lexical inference drawn from the 1974 dictionary's silence.

sources.citation: Lithgow, David. 1978. How should I spell it? Interpretation of problem sounds illustrated from Muyuw. In Richard Loving (ed.), Miscellaneous papers on Dobu and Arapesh, Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 25, 17-32. Ukarumpa: SIL. (SIL L&CA entry 23591)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.21: 'Muyuw words pattern differently when the stress or accent is on different syllables ... in the groups which are compared, the stress or accent should always be on the same syllable.' pp.22-24 'common pattern' lists carry an acute on the PENULTIMATE syllable in every polysyllabic noun given: two-syllable stems kʌ́nig, bʷélim, gʷélekʷ, yávig, wɔ́yim, tɔ́wos; three-syllable gʌmʌ́gal, tʌnúgʷeb, ligúlagʷ, likʷʌ́lekʷ, mitʌ́kʷabʷ, kʌyʌ́mat, yigʌ́yog, wulíyogʷ; tʌnmúnum, kʌlpʷákit, kʌwlʌ́vag; possessed muyávig, muwɔ́yim, dʌ́bans, ʌdkábɔls, mulgúlagʷ, dʌlgúlagʷs; kin nouns nʌ́tun, yʌ́wan, túwan.
sources.locator: p. 21 section 4 'Method of study'; pp. 22-24 sections 5-6 word-pattern lists with stress marked; p. 31 section 12 'Words' (page images viewed)
sources.note: Published orthography/phonology paper by the same author with stress-marked 'common pattern' word lists (pp. 22-24, uniformly penultimate on nouns) and a word-prosody statement (p. 31); the only published phonological treatment of Muyuw beyond the dictionary front-matter.

sources.quote: 'The occurrence of allomorphic variants of verbal affixes depends upon stress placement, vowel harmony and morphological classification' (4.); subject-prefix allomorphs 'occur when the verb stem is unstressed / stressed' (4.3); 'í-siw I-enter / i-síw I-stay away (These two verb stems are identical apart from stress-placement)'; 4.4 final stem vowel lost unless plural morpheme occurs with penultimate-stressed stem. Treats stress placement as given; states no default position. Adds one surface stress-only lexical pair among verbs.
sources.locator: section 4 'Morphophonemics', printed pp. 15-17 (PDF pp. 20-22); errata sheet PDF p. 23
sources.note: Morphophonemics section conditions affix allomorphy on stress placement and gives a stress-only verb pair (í-siw / i-síw); background for the morphological-stress note, silent on default position.
